chunks: I wrote to Abu al-Hasan the Third (peace be upon him), asking him about the vision (of God) and what the people differ about regarding it. So he wrote:
The sighting is not possible unless there is air between the seer and the seen that the sight does not penetrate through.
So when the air is cut off from between the seer and the seen, the sighting is not valid, and there would be confusion in that.

Because whenever the seer equals the seen in the necessitating condition between them for vision, the confusion becomes obligatory, and that would be anthropomorphism (tashbih), because causes must inevitably be connected to their effects.

key_terms.التَّشْبِيه: Tashbih — anthropomorphism; likening God to created beings, which is rejected in Shia theology
key_terms.الرَّائِي: The seer/observer — the subject of the act of seeing
key_terms.الرُّؤْيَة: Vision/sighting — the theological question of whether God can be seen (beatific vision); a major point of controversy between Sunni schools and Shia theology
key_terms.الِاتِّصَال: Connection/linkage — the causal relationship between causes (asbab) and their effects (musabbabat)
key_terms.الِاشْتِبَاه: Confusion/similarity — the logical consequence that seer and seen become indistinguishable when conditions are equal
key_terms.الْمَرْئِيّ: The seen/object of vision — that which is perceived

ai.seo_question: What did Imam al-Hadi say about the possibility of seeing God?
ai.summary: Imam Ali al-Hadi (AS), the tenth Imam, responds in writing to Ahmad ibn Ishaq's question about the controversy over whether God can be seen (ru'yah). The Imam employs an optical-philosophical argument: physical vision requires an intervening medium (air) through which sight penetrates; if no such medium exists, vision fails. He then argues that if the seer and seen share the same causal conditions for vision, they become indistinguishable — which would imply that God is like created beings (tashbih, anthropomorphism), an impossibility. This response is a classic Shia theological refutation of the Sunni Mu'tazilite/Ash'arite debate on the beatific vision, affirming that God transcends spatial categories.
